audience.programmeDescription: Forest and Nature Conservation combines ecology and biodiversity with the social relationships, policy and management of forests, natural areas and landscapes.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Three UCR programmes develop related interests through different priorities: ecological and social conservation questions, environmental investigation, or policy and institutions. Specialist forestry, structured conservation fieldwork and the required Wageningen thesis remain important differences.

notes.text: The UCR programmes combine conservation, environmental systems and governance in different ways. They do not reproduce the full tree and forest-management sequence, specialist protected-area planning, compulsory joint ecological/social field courses or required 12-credit thesis. Optional UCR research is additional to each 180-credit schedule.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Public Economics
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Econometrics
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Living with Water
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Studies water risks and opportunities in deltas, using Zeeland as a central case. Flooding, freshwater scarcity, salinisation, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, then apply these ideas through site-based inquiry and a project on delta adaptation.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Introduces the diversity of living organisms, from bacteria and archaea to protists, plants, fungi and animals. Students examine evolutionary relationships, distinguishing characteristics and ecological roles. Practical work introduces microscopy, organism identification and biodiversity measurement, supported by a small project on a selected branch of the tree of life.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Conservation Biology
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Examines human-driven biodiversity loss and approaches to conservation. Students study habitat destruction, overharvesting, invasive species, climate change and extinction, followed by conservation planning and species management. A local threatened-species project investigates conservation status and protection measures and develops a public-awareness flyer.

selectedCourseDescriptions.name: Marine Biology
selectedCourseDescriptions.text: Marine Biology examines how marine ecosystems work and how people affect them. Students study ocean processes, marine microbes and habitats including estuaries, coasts and the deep sea. Seminars address issues such as fisheries, ocean acidification and plastic pollution. A multimedia project communicates a marine biology topic to a public audience.
